entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18711"/><div sID="gen39671" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18711"/><hi type="bold">4. Behold--</hi>calling attention to their coming doom as no vain threat.<div eID="gen39671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">labourers--</hi>literally "workmen."<div eID="gen39672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of you kept back--</hi>So English Version rightly. Not as Alford, "crieth out from you." The "keeping back of the hire" was, on the part OF the rich, virtually an act of "fraud," because the poor laborers were not immediately paid. The phrase is therefore not, "kept back by you," but "of you"; the latter implying virtual, rather than overt, fraud. James refers to <reference osisRef="Deut.24.14">De 24:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.15">15</reference>, "At this day ... give his hire, neither shall the sun go down upon it, lest he CRY against thee unto the Lord, and it be sin unto thee." Many sins "cry" to heaven for vengeance which men tacitly take no account of, as unchastity and injustice [Bengel]. Sins peculiarly offensive to God are said to "cry" to Him. The rich ought to have given freely to the poor; their not doing so was sin. A still greater sin was their not paying their debts. Their greatest sin was not paying them to the poor, whose wages is their all.<div eID="gen39673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cries of them--</hi>a double cry; both that of the hire abstractly, and that of the laborers hired.<div eID="gen39674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord of sabaoth--</hi>here only in the New Testament. In <reference osisRef="Rom.9.29">Ro 9:29</reference> it is a quotation. It is suited to the Jewish tone of the Epistle. It reminds the rich who think the poor have no protector, that the Lord of the whole hosts in heaven and earth is the guardian and avenger of the latter. He is identical with the "coming Lord" Jesus (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.7">Jas 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen39675" type="x-p"/>

Translate, "Ye have luxuriated ... and wantoned." The former expresses luxurious effeminacy; the latter, wantonness and prodigality. Their luxury was at the expense of the defrauded poor (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jas 5:4</reference>).<div eID="gen39676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on the earth--</hi>The same earth which has been the scene of your wantonness, shall be the scene of the judgment coming on you: instead of earthly delights ye shall have punishments.<div eID="gen39677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nourished ... hearts--</hi>that is glutted your bodies like beasts to the full extent of your hearts' desire; ye live to eat, not eat to live.<div eID="gen39678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39679" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as in a day of slaughter--</hi>The oldest authorities omit "as." Ye are like beasts which eat to their hearts' content on the very day of their approaching slaughter, unconscious it is near. The phrase answers to "the last days," <reference osisRef="Jas.5.3">Jas 5:3</reference>, which favors Alford's translation there, "in," not "for." <div eID="gen39679" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18713"/><div sID="gen39680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18713"/><hi type="bold">6. Ye have condemned ... the just--</hi>The Greek aorist expresses, "Ye are accustomed to condemn ... the just." Their condemnation of Christ, "the Just," is foremost in James' mind. But all the innocent blood shed, and to be shed, is included, the Holy Spirit comprehending James himself, called "the Just," who was slain in a tumult. See my Introduction. This gives a peculiar appropriateness to the expression in this verse, the same "as the righteous (just) man" (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.16">Jas 5:16</reference>). The justice or righteousness of Jesus and His people is what peculiarly provoked the ungodly great men of the world.<div eID="gen39680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he doth not resist you--</hi>The very patience of the Just one is abused by the wicked as an incentive to boldness in violent persecution, as if they may do as they please with impunity. God doth "resist the proud" (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.6">Jas 4:6</reference>); but Jesus as man, "as a sheep is dumb before the shearers, so He opened not His mouth": so His people are meek under persecution. The day will come when God will resist (literally, "set Himself in array against") His foes and theirs. <div eID="gen39681" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18714"/><div sID="gen39682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18714"/><hi type="bold">7. Be patient therefore--</hi>as judgment is so near (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.1">Jas 5:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.3">3</reference>), ye may well afford to be "patient" after the example of the unresisting Just one (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.6">Jas 5:6</reference>).<div eID="gen39682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brethren--</hi>contrasted with the "rich" oppressors, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.1-Jas.5.6">Jas 5:1-6</reference>.<div eID="gen39683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the coming of the Lord--</hi>Christ, when the trial of your patience shall cease.<div eID="gen39684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">husbandman waiteth for--</hi>that is, patiently bears toils and delays through hope of the harvest at last. Its "preciousness" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.126.6">Psa 126:6</reference>, "precious seed") will more than compensate for all the past. Compare the same image, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.3">Ga 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.9">9</reference>.<div eID="gen39685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39686" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath long patience for it--</hi>"over it," in respect to it.<div eID="gen39686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">until he receive--</hi>"until it receive" [Alford]. Even if English Version be retained, the receiving of the early and latter rains is not to be understood as the object of his hope, but the harvest for which those rains are the necessary preliminary. The early rain fell at sowing time, about November or December; the latter rain, about March or April, to mature the grain for harvest. The latter rain that shall precede the coming spiritual harvest, will probably be another Pentecost-like effusion of the Holy Ghost. <div eID="gen39687" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18715"/><div sID="gen39688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18715"/><hi type="bold">8. coming ... draweth nigh--</hi>The Greek expresses present time and a settled state. <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.7">1Pe 4:7</reference>, "is at hand." We are to live in a continued state of expectancy of the Lord's coming, as an event always nigh. Nothing can more "stablish the heart" amidst present troubles than the realized expectation of His speedy coming. <div eID="gen39688" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18716"/><div sID="gen39689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18716"/><hi type="bold">9. Grudge not--</hi>rather "Murmur not"; "grumble not." The Greek is literally, "groan": a half-suppressed murmur of impatience and harsh judgment, not uttered aloud or freely. Having exhorted them to patience in bearing wrongs from the wicked, he now exhorts them to a forbearing spirit as to the offenses given by brethren. Christians, who bear the former patiently, sometimes are impatient at the latter, though much less grievous.<div eID="gen39689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lest ... condemned--</hi>The best manuscript authorities read, "judged." James refers to <reference osisRef="Matt.7.1">Mt 7:1</reference>, "Judge not lest ye be judged." To "murmur against one another" is virtually to judge, and so to become liable to be judged.<div eID="gen39690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judge ... before the door--</hi>referring to <reference osisRef="Matt.24.33">Mt 24:33</reference>. The Greek is the same in both passages, and so ought to be translated here as there, "doors," plural. The phrase means "near at hand" (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Ge 4:7</reference>), which in the oldest interpretations [Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem] is explained, "thy sin is reserved unto the judgment of the world to come." Compare "the everlasting doors" (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.7">Psa 24:7</reference>, whence He shall come forth). The Lord's coming to destroy Jerusalem is primarily referred to; and ultimately, His coming again visibly to judgment. <div eID="gen39691" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18721"/><div sID="gen39710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18721"/><hi type="bold">14. let him call for the elders--</hi>not some one of the elders, as Roman Catholics interpret it, to justify their usage in extreme unction. The prayers of the elders over the sick would be much the same as though the whole Church which they represent should pray [Bengel].<div eID="gen39710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anointing him with oil--</hi>The usage which Christ committed to His apostles was afterwards continued with laying on of hands, as a token of the highest faculty of medicine in the Church, just as we find in <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1Co 6:2</reference> the Church's highest judicial function. Now that the miraculous gift of healing has been withdrawn for the most part, to use the sign where the reality is wanting would be unmeaning superstition. Compare other apostolic usages now discontinued rightly, 1Co 11:4-15; 16:<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.20">20</reference>. "Let them use oil who can by their prayers obtain recovery for the sick: let those who cannot do this, abstain from using the empty sign" [Whitaker]. Romish extreme unction is administered to those whose life is despaired of, to heal the soul, whereas James' unction was to heal the body. Cardinal Cajetan [Commentary] admits that James cannot refer to extreme unction. Oil in the East, and especially among the Jews (see the Talmud, Jerusalem and Babylon), was much used as a curative agent. It was also a sign of the divine grace. Hence it was an appropriate sign in performing miraculous cures.<div eID="gen39711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the name of the Lord--</hi>by whom alone the miracle was performed: men were but the instruments. <div eID="gen39712" type="x-p"/>

Elias ... like passions as we--</hi>therefore it cannot be said that he was so raised above us as to afford no example applicable to common mortals like ourselves.<div eID="gen39723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39724" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prayed earnestly--</hi>literally, "prayed with prayer": Hebraism for prayed intensely. Compare <reference osisRef="Luke.22.15">Lu 22:15</reference>, "With desire I have desired," that is, earnestly desired. Alford is wrong in saying, Elias' prayer that it might not rain "is not even hinted at in the Old Testament history." In <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.1">1Ki 17:1</reference> it is plainly implied, "As the Lord God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word." His prophecy of the fact was according to a divine intimation given to him in answer to prayer. In jealousy for God's honor (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.10">1Ki 19:10</reference>), and being of one mind with God in his abhorrence of apostasy, he prayed that the national idolatry should be punished with a national judgment, drought; and on Israel's profession of repentance he prayed for the removal of the visitation, as is implied in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.39-1Kgs.18.42">1Ki 18:39-42</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.4.25">Lu 4:25</reference>.<div eID="gen39724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">three years, &c.--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.1">1Ki 18:1</reference>, "The third year," namely, from Elijah's going to Zarephath; the prophecy (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.1">Jas 5:1</reference>) was probably about five or six months previously. <div eID="gen39725" type="x-p"/>

Elias ... like passions as we--therefore it cannot be said that he was so raised above us as to afford no example applicable to common mortals like ourselves. prayed earnestly--literally, "prayed with prayer": Hebraism for prayed intensely. Compare Lu 22:15, "With desire I have desired," that is, earnestly desired. Alford is wrong in saying, Elias' prayer that it might not rain "is not even hinted at in the Old Testament history." In 1Ki 17:1 it is plainly implied, "As the Lord God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word." His prophecy of the fact was according to a divine intimation given to him in answer to prayer. In jealousy for God's honor (1Ki 19:10), and being of one mind with God in his abhorrence of apostasy, he prayed that the national idolatry should be punished with a national judgment, drought; and on Israel's profession of repentance he prayed for the removal of the visitation, as is implied in 1Ki 18:39-42; compare Lu 4:25. three years, &c.--Compare 1Ki 18:1, "The third year," namely, from Elijah's going to Zarephath; the prophecy (Jas 5:1) was probably about five or six months previously.
